phase1.explanation:
[[term:Encapsulation]] is about deciding, on purpose, what parts of your blueprint the outside world is allowed to touch.

Java gives you four levels of [[term:access modifier]]s: `public` (anyone, anywhere), `private` (only inside this exact class), `protected` (this package plus subclasses), and no modifier at all, which defaults to package-level access.

[[key:The standard pattern is: make every field private, and expose controlled access through public getters and setters]]. A getter just hands back the current value — `getName()` returns `name`. A setter is where the real value comes in: it can validate before actually changing anything, like `setAge()` refusing any value outside 0–150 instead of blindly accepting it.

[[warn:Once a field is private, code outside the class genuinely cannot touch it directly]] — not `person.name`, not `person.age = 99`. That's not a limitation, that's the entire point: it forces every change to go through your validation logic instead of letting anything slip in unchecked.

Why bother with all this? Three real reasons: control over what values are actually allowed in, protection against your object ending up in some invalid state, and the freedom to change how something's stored internally later without breaking anyone else's code that calls your getters and setters.

phase2.explanation:
[[warn:This is encapsulation actually doing its job]] — `person.name` and `person.age` fail to compile specifically because those fields are `private`, and private genuinely means private: only code inside the `Person` class itself is allowed to touch them.

[[key:The fix isn't to make the fields public — it's to add public getters and setters]]: `getName()`/`setName(...)` for controlled access. That way outside code goes through `person.getName()` instead of `person.name`, and you keep the ability to validate or change internals later without breaking anything that calls those methods.

mcq.question:
What's the standard encapsulation pattern for a class's fields?

A) Make all fields public for easy access
B) Make fields private, expose access through public getters/setters
C) Make fields protected only
D) Avoid fields entirely

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a BankAccount class with:
• Private fields: owner (String), balance (double)
• Constructor
• Getters for both
• deposit(double amount) — adds to balance (must be positive)
• withdraw(double amount) — subtracts from balance (can't go negative)
• displayInfo() method

Test by creating an account and doing deposits/withdrawals.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the getX()/setX() naming pattern you just used isn't just a personal style choice — it's part of an actual Java convention called the JavaBeans specification. Plenty of tools and frameworks (form builders, serialization libraries, IDEs) specifically look for methods named exactly this way to automatically figure out what a class's properties are.
